nature-eco-129.title: Cattle outweigh wild mammals: measuring the human footprint
nature-eco-129.text: Domesticated cattle and pigs now outweigh all the world's wild mammals by 14 to 1. The world's chickens weigh three times as much as all wild birds. Numbers like these measure human impact on the environment: the changes people cause, directly or indirectly, to physical surroundings, ecosystems, biodiversity and natural resources. People have changed their surroundings ever since they first spread across the Earth. The impacts grew sharply after the Industrial Revolution of the 1700s. A 2018 study found 87% of the oceans altered by people, along with 77% of land outside Antarctica. Only 23% of the land was left as wilderness. Global Footprint Network estimates put humanity's demand 70% above what all the planet's ecosystems can regenerate. The damage is linked to growing populations, rapid economic growth, heavy consumption, pollution and forest clearing. It is also linked to harvesting resources faster than they renew, the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. The results include global warming, ocean acidification, the mass loss of species and the collapse of whole ecological systems, a form of {{ref:nature-found-023}}. At sea, a 2019 report by the panel described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}} blames one driver above all. Catching fish faster than they can breed is the main cause of the mass loss of ocean species.

nature-eco-041.title: Habitat destruction, the leading cause of species loss
nature-eco-041.text: The tropics once held about 16 million square kilometers of rainforest. Less than 9 million remain. That shrinkage is habitat destruction. A natural home for wildlife, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-294}}, becomes unable to support the species that live there, so they move away or die. It is the leading cause worldwide of lost biodiversity and of species dying out. People cause it through resource use, agriculture, industry, urban sprawl, mining, logging and fishing with trawl nets. A habitat need not be bulldozed to fail. Degradation, fragmentation and pollution can collapse it without outright destroying it. When habitat goes, the land can support fewer native animals, and each {{ref:nature-eco-374}} declines, sometimes until it disappears. Endemic species with small ranges suffer most because they live nowhere else. For people, the deepest cost is lost ecosystem services such as regulating climate, pollinating plants and managing water. Poor people suffer most. Wealthier people and countries can pay to keep receiving more than their share of natural resources.

nature-eco-053.title: Deforestation: trading forest for farms, ranches and towns
nature-eco-053.text: Forests cover about 31% of Earth's land. That is one-third less than before agriculture spread, and half of that loss came in the last century. Deforestation is the clearing of a forest or stand of trees so the land can serve a non-forest use, such as farms, ranches or towns. It is one of the main forms of {{ref:nature-eco-041}}. Between 2015 and 2020 it ran at an estimated 10 million hectares a year, down from 16 million a year in the 1990s. Agriculture is by far the main direct cause. In 2025 the spread of cropland and pasture drove nearly 90% of global deforestation. Logging, urbanization, mining and climate-driven wildfires add to it. Clearing destroys habitat, so it brings loss of biodiversity, species dying out, local climate change and the displacement of forest peoples. It also cuts the carbon forests take up, weakening their role in slowing climate change. Cleared regions often suffer soil erosion and the slide toward desert described in {{ref:nature-eco-091}}. The costs can dwarf the gains. In Brazil, economic losses from deforestation could reach around 317 billion dollars a year, about 7 times the value of the commodities it produces.

nature-eco-105.title: Extinction: when the last of a species dies
nature-eco-105.text: More than 99.9% of all the species that have ever lived are gone. The average species lasts 1–10 million years. Extinction is the end of a species, reached when its last member dies. The end can come before that last death, though. A species is functionally extinct once its few survivors can no longer reproduce and recover. The exact moment is hard to pin down over a large range, so extinction is usually declared after the fact. Life on Earth has passed through at least five mass extinctions. Fossil studies confirm that climate change has caused extinctions. A 2003 review predicted that 15–37% of land species would be 'committed to extinction' by 2050 because of climate change. Humans have become an extra cause, both as a new mega-predator and by moving animals and plants around the world. Today the main human cause is habitat degradation, and agriculture is the main cause of habitat degradation worldwide. In 2014 a special edition of the journal Science declared a widespread consensus that humans are driving mass species extinctions.

nature-eco-035.title: Biodiversity loss: a decline far faster than nature's pace
nature-eco-035.text: Between 1970 and 2016, monitored animal populations fell by an average of 68%, the WWF reported. The figure covered 4,400 animal species and nearly 21,000 populations. Biodiversity loss is the decline of living variety. It happens when species vanish from Earth entirely, as {{ref:nature-eco-105}} describes, or when they shrink or disappear from a particular area. To measure it at a site, scientists record the number of species present, a count explained in {{ref:nature-eco-150}}, and how it changes over time. The current global rate is estimated at 100 to 1000 times the natural background rate at which species die out, set out in {{ref:nature-eco-078}}. All of today's loss has been attributed to human activities. Habitat destruction, often for farming, is currently a bigger driver than climate change. The loss is temporary if the damage can be reversed, for example by repairing ecosystems as {{ref:nature-nbs-112}} describes, and permanent if it cannot. Damaged ecosystems provide poorer ecosystem services, such as pollinating crops, cleaning air and water, decomposing waste and supplying goods from forests. Governments have struggled to respond. Of 20 worldwide targets for biodiversity set in 2010, covered in {{ref:nature-gov-017}}, only six were partially achieved by 2020.

nature-eco-026.title: Invasive species: newcomers that harm their new home
nature-eco-026.text: An introduced species usually starts small. It has to persist at low densities first, and sometimes it takes several introductions before it takes hold. An invasive species is one that people have carried to a new place, where it harms the environment it has entered. Invasive species are the subset of established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity. Invasions happen naturally too, but human help has greatly increased their rate, scale and geographic range. Biological invasion is now one of the five top drivers of {{ref:nature-eco-035}} worldwide, and it is growing with tourism and globalization. Successful invaders share common traits: fast growth, rapid reproduction, association with humans and a record of earlier successful invasions. Scientific consensus holds that their effects on biodiversity are mainly negative. Some can still provide habitat or food for other organisms. The label itself is slippery, since "invasive" is poorly defined and often subjective.

nature-eco-140.title: Nature conservation: the movement to save what remains
nature-eco-140.text: The forester described in {{ref:nature-hist-061}} coined the term 'conservation' in 1907. Nature conservation is the ethic and movement devoted to saving species from extinction, keeping and restoring habitats, enhancing ecosystem services and protecting biodiversity. Its goals range widely: conserving habitat, preventing deforestation, keeping soil organic matter, halting extinctions, reducing the overharvesting of fish and slowing climate change. Its early choices were shaped by money. The first parks often protected 'worthless lands' of little commercial interest, such as alpine and dry habitats. As of 2018, 15% of land and 7.3% of the oceans were protected. Many environmentalists aim to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030. Money and management still lag behind. Reserves in developing countries, home to perhaps 70–80% of the world's species, get very little effective management. Private fundraising is not enough to pay for managing the more than 10% of the world that is legally protected.

nature-eco-063.title: Overexploitation: taking more than nature can replace
nature-eco-063.text: About 40% of the bird species lost since 1500 were affected by overexploitation. The word means harvesting a resource that renews itself, such as fish, forests, groundwater or wildlife, faster than it can replenish, to the point of diminishing returns. A {{ref:nature-eco-374}} is overexploited when it is harvested faster than its natural births and deaths can make up. That can wipe out populations or whole species. Ecologists count it among the five main activities threatening biodiversity worldwide, and it threatens one-third of endangered vertebrates. Excluding edible fish, the illegal trade in wildlife is valued at $10 billion a year. The same logic applies beyond animals. An underground water store is overexploited when water is pumped out faster than it recharges, and it is then said to be overdrafted. Forests are overexploited when logging outpaces the regrowth of trees. Harvesting can be sustainable if it stays within limits, as well-managed fishing grounds show. Why do people overharvest at all? Hardin's tragedy of the commons explains how people sharing a resource, each acting in self-interest, can overexploit and destroy it.

nature-nbs-115.title: Habitat fragmentation: when one wild place becomes many islands
nature-nbs-115.text: Keep 10% of a habitat as one unbroken remnant and, as a rough rule, half its biodiversity is lost. Habitat fragmentation is the breaking up of a large, continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches. It splits populations and degrades ecosystems. Five changes come bundled together. There is less total habitat and less interior compared with edge. Fragments are cut off from each other, one patch splits into several, and patches get smaller on average. People cause it by clearing native vegetation for farms, rural development, cities and hydroelectric reservoirs. Dams and water diversions do the same to rivers and lakes. Fragmentation consistently reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75%. It also impairs ecosystem functions such as biomass production and nutrient cycling. Small, isolated populations are fragile. Minor swings in climate or resources that a large population would absorb can wipe them out. The damage is slow to show, and experiments find biodiversity and ecosystem functioning still declining 20 or more years later. Linking fragments with corridors of native vegetation, bridges or underpasses can ease isolation, as {{ref:nature-eco-152}} explains. It does not restore interior habitat.

nature-eco-060.title: Land degradation: when land loses its power to produce
nature-eco-060.text: Every year around 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded. Land degradation is the process by which land becomes less healthy and productive, through human activity or natural conditions. Unsustainable land management is often the main cause, and over 60% of human-induced degradation occurs on farmland. The UN estimates that about 30% of land is degraded worldwide, with about 3.2 billion people living in degrading areas. A major 2005 global review, {{ref:nature-es-001}}, defined it more narrowly, as the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of dry lands. Its effects spread outward. It lowers crop yields and ecosystem diversity, leaves land more exposed to floods and droughts, and releases greenhouse gases. Degraded land is also less resilient, so further shocks can drive still more degradation. The flip side is hopeful. Reversing 10% of human-induced cropland degradation could feed an additional 154 million people a year.

nature-eco-091.title: Desertification: how dry land turns to desert
nature-eco-091.text: Dry regions cover about 40–41% of Earth's land and are home to more than 2 billion people, at least 90% of them in developing countries. Desertification is the gradual degradation of fertile land in those regions into desert, through natural processes and human activities. It is the harshest form of {{ref:nature-eco-060}}. The immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation. Drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees for fuel or building all strip it away. Bare dry soil then blows or washes off, leaving infertile layers that bake into unproductive hardpan. Some 10–20% of dry regions are already degraded, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification. Climate change is expected to expand dry regions from 38% of continental land in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by 2100. Remedies exist: shelter belts and woodlots, planted lines and blocks of trees, fix soil and cut erosion. Yet the economics can work against them. Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when they benefit society and the environment.

nature-eco-118.title: Genetic diversity: a species' insurance against change
nature-eco-118.text: Koalas carry little genetic variety, and that weakness is linked to their failure to fight off chlamydia. Genetic diversity is the total variety of inherited characteristics within a species. It lets populations adapt to changing environments, because some individuals are more likely to carry variants suited to new conditions. Lower diversity leaves a population more exposed to changes such as climate change or new diseases. Small populations lose diversity by chance, a process called genetic drift, and through inbreeding. A bottleneck, a sudden crash in numbers, can cut it rapidly. Mutation and gene flow, such as pollen carried by wind or migrating birds, add new variants. A 2007 study found that diversity within species and diversity among species depend on each other. In farm animals, the loss of genetic diversity has been attributed to the spread of markets and economic globalization.

nature-eco-150.title: Species richness: counting how many kinds live here
nature-eco-150.text: The simplest measure of nature's variety is a headcount of kinds. Species richness is the number of different species in a community, landscape or region. It ignores how common each species is. That makes it different from a fuller measure that also weighs how evenly individuals are shared among species, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-147}}. Larger samples tend to contain more species, so richness values can be compared only when sampling effort is standardized. Many groups of organisms have the most species in the tropics, so richness changes with latitude. Conservationists often use it to judge a habitat's value, but it is blind to which species are present. Areas with many endemic or rare species usually count for more. How richness relates to an ecosystem's productivity is unsettled: studies disagree, and no global consensus has emerged.

nature-eco-152.title: Wildlife corridors: reconnecting cut-off populations
nature-eco-152.text: In a South Carolina experiment, butterflies were two to four times more likely to move to a patch linked by a corridor than to unlinked patches. A wildlife corridor is an area that links wildlife populations cut off from each other by farms, cities, roads and other development. It eases the harm of {{ref:nature-nbs-115}}, a major threat to biodiversity. When animals can move between populations, isolated groups avoid inbreeding and the loss of genetic diversity, and pollen and seeds spread. Corridors joining warmer and cooler habitat help species shift their ranges as the climate changes. They can be continuous strips of habitat or 'stepping stones' of small separate patches, and they include river zones and road crossings. Success needs a shared vision among stakeholders, clear rules and incentive programs to bring in private landowners. Corridors can also lead wildlife into settlements, causing conflicts such as crop raiding and attacks on livestock.

nature-eco-069.title: Abundance: how common a species is
nature-eco-069.text: In most ecosystems a few species are common and many are rare. Abundance measures how well represented a species is in a particular ecosystem, usually counted as individuals per sample. Relative species abundance compares one species with the others around it, and both measures feed into biodiversity calculations. Counting methods vary. Large animals are counted with spotlights, tracks and even roadkill, while plants are often measured by the share of a plot they cover. Abundant species tend to be generalists that use many resources, and rare ones specialists with narrow needs. Abundant species also produce more colonizing offspring. That loop yields widespread core species and scarce satellite species.

nature-eco-103.title: Endemism: species found in one place only
nature-eco-103.text: Charles Darwin first used the word "endemic" in 1872, for a species restricted to one place. Endemism is the state of a species being found naturally in only one defined place, such as a single island, country or region. Its opposite is a cosmopolitan distribution, a global or widespread range. Isolation breeds endemics, so remote islands such as Hawaii, the Galápagos and Socotra hold many. Endemic does not mean rare, and rare does not mean endemic. Small ranges do raise the stakes: endemics face greater risk than widespread species from habitat loss and fast climate change. Conservation biology uses endemism to measure a place's biodiversity, judge extinction risk and set priorities, the idea behind {{ref:nature-eco-081}}. Some scientists argue it is a poor guide, because high-endemism areas do not consistently match high biodiversity or high threat.

nature-eco-066.title: Forests and climate: a feedback loop of loss
nature-eco-066.text: Standing forests in the tropics help cool the global average temperature by more than 1 °C. Clearing them works the other way. Changing how land is used, mainly through deforestation, is the second largest human source of carbon dioxide after burning fossil fuels. The emissions come from burning the wood and leaves of forests and from decomposing plant material and soil carbon. As of 2019, deforestation caused about 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year. That service is weakening. In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of heat, drought and deforestation. The link runs both ways, as a self-amplifying loop. More tree loss means more warming, which brings more wildfires, pests and storms, and so more tree loss. Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and the collapse of forest ecosystems.

nature-eco-144.title: Poaching: illegal hunting and its ripple effects
nature-eco-144.text: As many as 35,000 African elephants are killed each year for their ivory. Poaching is the illegal hunting or capture of wild animals, and since the 1980s also the illegal harvesting of wild plants. It is an unlawful form of {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. In rural Africa the main motives are a lack of jobs and limited farming potential, and selling wild meat to cities brings cash. International markets draw organized gangs, and crime syndicates traffic body parts abroad. Poachers treat the edges of reserves as open-access resources, free for anyone to take. That shrinks the reserves' effective size, and wildlife tourism loses income. Removing large animals also changes how seeds are spread, so large-seeded trees come to dominate and small-seeded plants vanish locally. A UN goal, {{ref:nature-gov-030}}, calls for action against the poaching and trafficking of protected species. The label is contested: critics argue it has been used to criminalize Indigenous peoples' traditional subsistence hunting.

nature-eco-123.title: The 2019 global assessment: a million species at risk
nature-eco-123.text: Of an estimated 8 million animal and plant species, 1 million are threatened with extinction. That was the headline of the Global Assessment Report, whose summary for policymakers came out on 6 May 2019. It was produced by the panel described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}}. It reviews 50 years of change, drawing on over 15,000 scientific publications and Indigenous knowledge. It was the UN's first worldwide assessment of biodiversity since the 2005 review covered in {{ref:nature-es-001}}. The threatened include 40% of amphibians and more than a third of marine mammals. Wild mammal biomass has fallen by 82%, while humans and their farm animals now make up 96% of all mammal biomass. Over the same 50 years the human population doubled and GDP per person quadrupled. The report ranked the drivers: changes in land and sea use, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive alien species. Pollinator loss threatens food worth $235 to $577 billion a year. The report urged countries not to fixate on economic growth and to shift government support away from industries that harm nature.

nature-eco-093.title: Diversity indices: boiling variety down to one number
nature-eco-093.text: Counting species tells only part of the story. A diversity index is a number that measures how many different types, usually species, a dataset or community contains, often weighted by how common each is. Indices summarize parts of biodiversity such as richness, evenness and dominance, so communities or sites are easy to compare. Richness, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-150}}, is a simple count of types. It is popular in ecology because data on abundance are often lacking. Abundance itself can be measured as numbers of individuals, biomass or coverage. The Shannon and Simpson indices also account for each type's share of the total. The same measures work outside ecology, for demographic groups or even letters of the alphabet.

nature-eco-081.title: Biodiversity hotspots: small areas, most of the species
nature-eco-081.text: Biodiversity hotspots cover just 2.4% of the planet's surface, yet they support nearly 60% of the world's plant, bird, mammal, reptile and amphibian species. A hotspot is a region with exceptionally high biodiversity, especially species found nowhere else, that is threatened by human activity. Norman Myers developed the idea in articles in 1988 and 1990, revised in 2000. The test is strict. A region must hold at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species, plants with veins that carry water, which is over 0.5% of the world total. It must also have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation. Globally, 36 zones qualify. Most are tropical, and only a small share of their land is protected. Critics note that the approach ignores the cost of conservation. It also ignores phylogenetic diversity, the variety of evolutionary lineages a place holds.

openers.biodiversity-and-its-loss: Every change people make to land and water reaches the living things that depend on it. This chapter follows those changes, from forests cleared for farms, ranches and towns to habitats broken into small, isolated patches. It traces how fertile land wears out, how dry regions slide toward desert, and how fish, forests and groundwater are taken faster than they can renew. The end point is loss: species that fade from one area, and species that vanish when their last member dies. Against this stands nature conservation, the movement to save species, restore habitats and protect the variety of life.
